newsitem.title: TANZANIA: Rwandan ex-mayor Akayesu on trial for genocide.
newsitem.headline: Rwandan ex-mayor Akayesu on trial for genocide.

text.p: The defendant on trial at the U.N. tribunal on Rwanda's 1994 genocide is a former school inspector and local mayor.
Jean-Paul Akayesu, from the majority Hutu tribe, is charged with crimes against humanity and genocide by the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda (ICTR) sitting in Arusha, Tanzania.
Akayesu, 43, pleaded not guilty. He faces life imprisonment if convicted by the U.N.-created tribunal.

His three-lawyer defence team was led on Thursday by Nicolas Taingaye, a barrister from the Central African Republic. But on Friday Akayesu immediately filed an application seeking to change his lawyers for the third time.
Akayesu's trial was adjourned last October to allow the defence more time to prepare its case.
The most well-dressed of the first three accused to appear before the tribunal, he usually wears a suit or jacket and tie and is attentive in court.
The following information is taken solely from the tribunal's indictment against Akayesu and from statements made to the tribunal.
At the start of Rwanda's genocide on April 6, 1994, Akayesu was bourgmestre, or local government representative, at Taba commune in Gitarama province.

He is charged with 10 counts of genocide, complicity in genocide, crimes against humanity, direct and public incitement to commit genocide, crimes against humanity (murder) and violations of Article Three common to the Geneva Conventions.
As bourgmestre, he was responsible for maintaining public order in Taba commune, subject to the authority of the prefect, the indictment says.
He had exclusive control over the communal police, as well as any gendarmes put at the disposition of the commune.

At least 2,000 members of the Tutsi minority were killed in Taba commune between April and the end of June 1994, the indictment says, adding the killings were openly committed and were so widespread that Akayesu must have known about them.

"Although he had the authority and responsibility to do so, Jean-Paul Akayesu never attempted to prevent the killing of Tutsis in his commune or called for assistance from regional or national authorities to quell the violence," it adds.

In particular, Akayesu is accused of failing to take steps on or about April 19, 1994, to have the killers of a teacher, Sylvere Karera, arrested despite at least one of the perpetrators being turned over to him, the indictment says.

He is accused of sanctioning Karera's death and urging a meeting of more than 100 people to eliminate accomplices of the Rwanda Patriotic Front (RPF), the mainly Tutsi rebels who took power in Rwanda after the genocide.
At the meeting in Gishyeshye sector, Akayesu named at least three prominent Tutsis he said had to be killed because of their alleged relationship with the RPF rebels, the charges say.
Within the next few days two of them had been killed.
Akayesu is charged with blowing a whistle to alert local residents to the attempted escape of three brothers. After they were captured, he allegedly ordered and took part in their killing.
The indictment says Akayesu took eight detained men from his office and ordered militia members to kill them. They were slaughtered with clubs, machetes, small axes and sticks.
Akayesu is accused of ordering local people and militiamen to kill intellectuals and influential people. Five teachers from Taba secondary school were allegedly killed on his orders.
During an interrogation on or about April 20, 1994, men under Akayesu's authority allegedly forced Victims Y and Z to beat each other and used a piece of Y's dress to strangle Z.
